title: Vermillion
content: The letter came up the switchback road on a boy's bicycle the morning the madder was boiling, and by noon every shutter in Ambry was pulled to the sill. It said the lower bridge was closed by order of the district, that the valley was sealed against the mumps coming up from the river towns, and that no one was to cross until the physicians sent word. Ysolde read it twice at the dye-house door, then folded it into her apron, because the wedding was on Saturday and the cloth on her frame was still only half red. Her mother had taught her that the color would not hold through the first rain unless it was set in the warm water that rose beneath the bathhouse, and the keeper had always let her fill two buckets at dusk. So at dusk she walked down the terrace steps past the wardens' rope, which had been tied to the wrong post and left a gap wide enough for a woman's shoulders. Inside, the steam was thick as wool, and the old floor tiles ran with a crack that followed the fault beneath them the way a stitch follows a fold. She filled her buckets at the basin under the tall oval mirror, because the spring came up cleanest there, and the water made a sound like someone talking to themselves in another room. Her reflection looked back at her, older than it had at breakfast, with her husband's set mouth, the mouth that had signed the loan thirty years ago without telling her. Beside her own shadow on the wet tiles lay a second one, thinner, leaning toward the buckets as if it wanted to drink first. She did not turn around. She carried the water up the steps, and it stayed warm against her palms the whole way, and the rope lay coiled where she had left it. At the frame she dipped the linen once, twice, and watched the red come up through the cloth like a bruise surfacing through skin, slow and then all at once. On the seventh dip the second shadow was in the weave too, a dark pull beneath the red, and she understood that the cloth was keeping it. She dipped the eighth time anyway, and when she lifted the linen out, the shadow hung off its edge like a hem, and she did not shake it loose.
premise: Ysolde wants to finish her daughter's vermillion wedding cloth before the road closes, but the sealing order has put the warm spring water she needs on the far side of a rope.

title: Chalk
content: The chalk had come from the schoolroom in a tin with a dented lid, and Teodor had kept it in his shirt since the wardens came up the road with the sealing notice. Inside the quarter the houses were shut and the children were kept behind the pump house, and his mother lay in the back room with a swelling in her jaw and a fever that made her talk to the window. The physician had written that the sickness would take her hearing before her breath, which was the sort of thing a physician wrote when he did not want to be asked again. Teodor's grandmother had been the last person in Ambry who could dete, which was to speak in the rhythm of the river so that the water carried the words down to the next village, and she had taught him the trick before her hands withered to sticks. "Chalk doors open onto whatever you cannot stop wanting," she told him once, "but they only take one through, and they never bring back what they did not ask for." He had thought she was telling one of her stories, the ones about the valley past the mill where every sound came back to you from a different direction, and where, she said, the echoes lived on with nobody left to keep them. He drew the door on the wall beside the back-room window, a tall rectangle with a round handle low on the right, and worked the chalk until the lines were black and his fingers grey to the knuckle. Then he dete'd the rhythm against the stone, quietly, the way she had shown him, and the wall gave a sound like wind across the mouth of a bottle and the outline went faintly warm. The door opened inward onto grass and mist, and the mist was full of voices calling back and forth, his own among them, arriving a half-second late from three directions at once. His mother lay with her eyes shut, and when he said her name the room said it back to him from the far hills. He could go through, find the physician in the next village, and bring back the medicine waiting in a box at the district office. But the door would take only one person, and it seemed the chalk had settled the matter before he had. He stood with one foot on the threshold of the grass and watched his mother's breath come short and whistling. Then he stepped back into the room, pulled the door shut, and wrote her name on the brass handle the way the schoolmaster wrote names on slates. He pressed his palm flat against it until the chalk was warm and smeared, and his hand came away the same grey as hers.
premise: Teodor wants to get his mother out of the sealed quarter before the sickness takes her, but the only door he can draw opens onto the valley, and it will carry only one person through.

title: Wras
content: Ansel had kept the ledger for thirty-one years, and for the last four months he had written in it what he measured at night with a plumb line and a candle: the width of the crack in the caldarium, the depth to which the spring had dropped, the water gone from scalding to tepid in a single week. He did not write the word fault. He wrote numbers under a column headed Maintenance, kept the figures honest, and kept the baths open, because the baths were what Ambry lived on through the cold months, and because a closed bathhouse would have looked like the confession he had not made. His daughter Liesl was to marry the paper-mill man's son on Saturday, and the whole valley had come to the banns with its best linen and its questions. Ansel had put off telling anyone the way a man puts off a letter he knows will end a friendship. Now the district had sealed the valley, the wardens stood at the bridge with their rope, and the town had gone quiet the way a kitchen goes quiet when someone has dropped a plate in another room. At night the building made a sound the old men called the wras, the sound a house makes when no one is listening, and he had been hearing it all winter under the pipes and the tick of cooling tile. He carried the ledger down to the furnace room where the coal fire ran the boilers, and opened it on the iron ledge beside the grate. The first page was dry, and the second had curled at the corner from the heat of his hand. He read the numbers aloud, slowly, because a thing spoken to an empty room is at least a kind of confession, and then he tore each page free and laid it on the coals. The paper browned at its edges, then lit with a small blue hiss, and the figures went up the flue like sparks from a wedding, white and quick. Halfway through he heard Liesl's voice at the top of the steps, calling for him in the bright tone she had used since she was small, the one that assumed he would be there. He did not answer. He fed the last page to the fire, the one with the date of the first crack, and the flame took it the way a bride takes a ring, without hesitating. Then he climbed the stairs with the empty ledger under his arm, crossed the tiled hall, and lifted the lamp to the tall oval mirror. The man in the glass lifted his lamp too, slowly, as if he had been waiting a long time for the first of them to tell the truth.
premise: Ansel the bath keeper wants to tell the town that the fault has moved beneath the baths, but the only one who will listen is the daughter he has spent his life shielding from the truth.
